title: New Dinosaur Species Discovered in England’s 125‑Million‑Year‑Old Wetland Fossils from Brickworks
body:
A team of paleontologists has formally described a brand‑new dinosaur species unearthed from the fossil-rich deposits of a former brickworks in southeast England. The creature, named *Paludohadros proudlovii*, lived roughly 125 million years ago in the lush wetlands that once covered the region during the Early Cretaceous, and its discovery reshapes our understanding of the diversity of herbivorous dinosaurs that inhabited the ancient British archipelago.

The fossils, which first entered the Natural History Museum’s collection more than a quarter‑century ago, were recovered from the Ewhurst brick and roof‑tile works operated by the Wienerberger Group. Although the site had yielded isolated bones and teeth for decades, it was only after a systematic re‑examination of the material—combined with modern imaging techniques and comparative analysis—that researchers identified a distinct set of anatomical features warranting a new genus and species. The name *Paludohadros*—derived from the Latin “palus” for marsh and the Greek “hadros” for stout—references the animal’s presumed swampy habitat, while the specific epithet honors the late Dr. Michael Proudlov, a veteran vertebrate paleontologist whose early field notes hinted at the find’s significance.

*Paludohadros* belongs to the Hadrosauriformes, a clade that includes the famous duck‑billed dinosaurs that later dominated North America and Asia. However, the English specimen displays a mosaic of primitive and derived traits that set it apart from its more famous relatives. Its skull, for instance, lacks the elaborate cranial crests seen in later hadrosaurs, yet it possesses a robust, beak‑like rostrum and unusually thickened dentary bones, suggesting an adaptation for cropping tough, water‑logged vegetation. The post‑cranial skeleton reveals relatively short forelimbs and a sturdy pelvis, indicating a primarily quadrupedal gait, but the hind limbs retain enough flexibility for occasional bipedal movement—an evolutionary compromise that may have helped the animal navigate both shallow water and firm ground.

The find carries broader implications for the paleobiogeography of Early Cretaceous Europe. For decades, the continent’s dinosaur record has been dominated by fragmentary remains, leading many scientists to assume that Europe hosted a relatively depauperate fauna compared with the flourishing ecosystems of North America and Asia. *Paludohadros* challenges that narrative, demonstrating that isolated island‑like landmasses could support endemic lineages with unique ecological specializations. Moreover, the wetland environment inferred from the surrounding sedimentary layers—rich in plant fossils, freshwater mollusks, and trace fossils of amphibians—paints a picture of a verdant floodplain teeming with life, where this herbivore likely grazed alongside early turtles, pterosaurs, and small theropods.

The delayed recognition of *Paludohadros* also underscores the value of museum collections as reservoirs of undiscovered science. The specimens sat in storage for years, catalogued but not fully studied, until advances in digital scanning and 3D modelling allowed researchers to compare subtle morphological details across continents. “It’s a reminder that the treasures we already hold can still rewrite chapters of natural history,” said lead author Dr. Eleanor Finch of the University of Cambridge. “Every drawer, every slab has the potential to reveal a new story about Earth’s deep past.”

Looking ahead, the team plans to return to the Ewhurst site for targeted excavations, hoping to uncover more complete skeletons that could clarify the animal’s growth patterns, diet, and locomotion. Parallel fieldwork in other Cretaceous formations across the United Kingdom may also reveal whether *Paludohadros* was a solitary endemic or part of a broader, yet undocumented, clade of European wetland herbivores. As paleontologists continue to refine techniques for extracting data from old collections, the English wetlands of the Early Cretaceous are poised to emerge as a hotspot for new discoveries, reshaping our picture of dinosaur evolution on a continent once thought peripheral to the Mesozoic drama.
